entry.title: Coalescing Concurrent Work with Singleflight
entry.summary: Use Asyncband's singleflight Group to let overlapping calls share one execution, handle errors and cancellation, and choose between the group and the once family by whether results are retained.
entry.content:
Concurrent callers sometimes need the same expensive result at the same time: a short-lived credential that several requests must refresh, a remote directory that several operations need to exist, or a report that several queries want built. Running the work once per caller multiplies load on whatever produces the result, and every caller waits for its own duplicate execution.

Asyncband's singleflight::Group coalesces these calls: while work for a key is in flight, later callers for that key wait and, on success, receive a clone of the value. This post covers sharing one execution, what happens when the shared execution fails or is cancelled, and how to choose between a group and the once family, whose members retain completed state.

The Asyncband APIs below are from version 0.7.3, with the singleflight features enabled.

Share one execution per key​

A group coalesces by key. work takes a key and an async function; while the function for that key is running, later calls with the same key wait for its result instead of starting their own:

use asyncband::singleflight::Group;

struct Credentials {
    refreshes: Group<&'static str, String>,
}

impl Credentials {
    async fn refresh_token(&self) -> String {
        self.refreshes
            .work("token", || async {
                // one round trip to the issuer, no matter how many callers overlap
                issue_token().await
            })
            .await
    }
}

Three callers that overlap run issue_token once. The first executes the function; the other two wait and each receive a clone of its value, so the value type must be Clone. Share an Arc<T> when the value is large or cloned often.

Keys are independent: calls with different keys never share an execution. A group does not limit overall concurrency; it collapses duplicate executions for the same key.

No cache after completion​

When the function completes successfully, the group removes the key. A call that starts after the previous one finished executes its own function again. For the token sample this means that calls which do not overlap each issue a token. A real refresh path caches the token until near expiry and enters the group only on a cache miss; the group itself holds no value over for later calls.

When later callers should reuse a completed result, either compose the group with a cache of your own or use the once family below. The two production users at the end of this post both compose: the group collapses overlapping calls, and a separate cache retains the result for later callers.

Errors, cancellation, and retries​

work takes an infallible function. Use try_work when the function can fail: it takes a function returning Result<V, E> and returns Result<V, E> to the caller.

An error is returned only to the caller that ran the function, not shared with callers that joined. After an error, or if the active call is cancelled or panics, the next waiting caller takes over and runs its own function while any remaining callers keep waiting. The same key can therefore execute more than once while attempts fail.

The function must not call work or try_work for its own key: it would wait for its own result. Calls for other keys proceed independently.

forget detaches a key's in-flight execution. Calls that already joined it keep their result; later callers start a fresh execution even while the old one is still running. Use it when an in-flight call is taking too long and newer callers should not queue behind it.

Choosing between a group and the Once family​

Asyncband's Once family retains completed state; a group does not. The members differ in what they retain:

Asyncband APIAfter completionUse
singleflight::GroupThe key is removed; a later call executes again.Overlapping calls for a key share one execution.
OnceMapThe value is retained until remove or discard.Compute once per key and cache the result.
OnceCellThe value is retained.Store one value from an initializer supplied at access time.
LazyCellThe value is retained.Initialize one value with a stored function; the in-flight future survives caller cancellation.
OnceNo value is stored.Run a side effect once, without storing a value.

OnceMap is the retained counterpart of a group. Its compute runs the function once per key and serves every later caller a clone of the stored value, until remove or discard drops the entry, after which the next call computes again. try_compute takes a Result-returning function, mirroring try_work on a group. Every successful lookup returns an owned clone of the value, so prefer Arc<T> entries when values are large or frequently shared.

Failed, cancelled, or panicked attempts leave OnceCell and OnceMap entries available for another attempt. Once is likewise infallible, and a cancelled or panicked run is abandoned the same way: a later call runs again. LazyCell instead preserves the same in-flight future across caller cancellation, and a panic poisons the cell rather than starting another attempt.

In production​

Reqsign signs Azure Storage requests with user delegation keys. Because the keys expire, a burst of signing requests can simultaneously find the cached key missing. Reqsign keeps one group for these refreshes: on a cache miss, callers enter try_work with a key covering the cache entry and its validity window, so overlapping misses issue one request to Azure. The closure re-checks the cache before sending the request in case another call populated a usable key after the initial miss, and a failed request returns its error to the executing caller while letting a joined caller retry. However, Reqsign writes the fetched key to the cache after try_work returns: a caller arriving after the flight finishes but before that write lands misses both the flight and the cache, issuing a second request unless the write completes before its closure's re-check runs.

OpenDAL's Google Drive backend creates directories on demand, where concurrent operations on the same path would otherwise each query or create the same directory. The backend keys a group by the parent directory's ID and the new directory's name, re-checking the path index inside try_work before querying or creating the directory. Unlike Reqsign's after-return write, OpenDAL inserts the resolved ID into the path index before the shared execution returns: publishing inside the flight ensures that on success there is never a gap where the flight is gone and the index is still empty.

For work that overlapping callers can share, a group collapses the duplicates and retains nothing. Combine it with a cache when later callers should reuse the result, or choose the once family when retention is the primary need.

entry.title: Moving from tokio::sync to Asyncband
entry.summary: How channel backpressure, semaphore acquisition, notifications, and initialization change when you migrate from tokio::sync to Asyncband.
entry.content:
You can keep the Tokio runtime when you switch synchronization primitives. Consider what happens when a bounded broadcast channel fills: Tokio lets a slow receiver miss messages, while Asyncband can make the sender wait for that receiver.

The examples use Tokio 1.53.3 and Asyncband 0.7.3. Asyncband has no default features; enable the features you need in Cargo.toml. For example, to use Asyncband's broadcast channel:

[dependencies.asyncband]
version = "=0.7.3"
features = ["broadcast"]

Channels​

Broadcast​

Tokio's bounded broadcast channel evicts the oldest message when a send would overflow the buffer. A receiver that missed that message gets RecvError::Lagged on its next receive:

let (tx, mut rx) = tokio::sync::broadcast::channel(1);

tx.send(1).unwrap();
tx.send(2).unwrap();

assert!(matches!(
    rx.recv().await,
    Err(tokio::sync::broadcast::error::RecvError::Lagged(1))
));

Asyncband's broadcast::mpmc::bounded keeps a message until each receiver that was subscribed when it was sent has read it or unsubscribed. When the buffer fills, send(value).await waits for space. Here the fast receiver has already read the first message, but try_send(2) still fails until the slow receiver reads it too:

use asyncband::broadcast::mpmc::{self, TrySendError};

let (tx, mut fast) = mpmc::bounded(1);
let mut slow = tx.subscribe();

tx.try_send(1).unwrap();
assert_eq!(fast.try_recv(), Ok(1));
assert!(matches!(tx.try_send(2), Err(TrySendError::Full(2))));

assert_eq!(slow.try_recv(), Ok(1));
tx.try_send(2).unwrap();

The send result also changes. Tokio's send() returns a receiver count on success or SendError if there are no receivers. Asyncband's bounded send().await returns () and retains nothing if there are no receivers.

MPSC​

Replace Tokio's mpsc::channel(capacity) with mpsc::bounded(capacity). For an unbounded channel, replace unbounded_channel() with unbounded().

- let (tx, mut rx) = tokio::sync::mpsc::channel::<u32>(16);
+ let (tx, mut rx) = asyncband::mpsc::bounded::<u32>(16);

After all senders have been dropped, both channels still deliver buffered messages. Once the buffer is empty, Tokio's recv() returns None; Asyncband's returns Err(RecvError::Disconnected):

use asyncband::mpsc::{self, RecvError};

let (tx, mut rx) = mpsc::bounded(1);
tx.send(42).await.unwrap();
drop(tx);

assert_eq!(rx.recv().await, Ok(42));
assert_eq!(rx.recv().await, Err(RecvError::Disconnected));

Watch​

Tokio's borrow() and borrow_and_update() return read guards. Asyncband's get() clones the latest value without marking it seen. Use recv().await to wait for an unseen version, clone the value, and mark that version seen in one call. Intermediate updates can be coalesced.

- let value = rx.borrow().clone();
+ let value = rx.get();

- rx.changed().await?;
- let value = rx.borrow_and_update().clone();
+ let value = rx.recv().await?;

Oneshot​

Both receivers support rx.await. The difference shows up in a select! loop: Tokio's receiver implements Future, while Asyncband's implements IntoFuture. Convert it once before the loop so a timer tick can win without discarding the pending receive. Import IntoFuture explicitly for Rust 2021 callers.

+ use std::future::IntoFuture;
+
- let mut recv = rx;
+ let mut recv = rx.into_future();

  loop {
      tokio::select! {
          result = &mut recv => {
              handle(result?);
              break;
          }
          _ = tick.tick() => {}
      }
  }

Semaphore​

Replace Tokio's acquire().await? with acquire(1).await for a single permit. For a batch, Tokio's acquire_many takes a u32; Asyncband's acquire takes a usize and returns a guard directly:

  let n: u32 = 3;
- let permits = semaphore.acquire_many(n).await?;
+ let permits = semaphore.acquire(usize::try_from(n)?).await;

The remaining ? handles the integer conversion. If your count is already a usize, pass it directly.

Tokio's Semaphore::close() makes pending and subsequent acquire calls fail with AcquireError. Asyncband has no closed state: a request that cannot be satisfied can wait indefinitely. If you relied on closure to stop workers, select between acquisition and a shutdown request.

To add capacity, replace Tokio's add_permits(n) with Asyncband's release(n). Here the semaphore starts empty, but the permit is available by the time acquire(1) runs:

let sem = asyncband::semaphore::Semaphore::new(0);
assert!(sem.try_acquire(1).is_none());

sem.release(1);
let permit = sem.acquire(1).await;
assert_eq!(permit.permits(), 1);

Adjusting capacity​

Asyncband's drain_permits(n), like Tokio's forget_permits(n), removes only currently available permits and returns the number removed. Use reduce_permits(n) to shrink the budget even when permits are checked out. Here draining removes nothing; reducing by three leaves five permits once the guard is dropped:

use asyncband::semaphore::Semaphore;

let sem = Semaphore::new(8);
let held = sem.acquire(8).await;

assert_eq!(sem.drain_permits(3), 0);
sem.reduce_permits(3);
drop(held);

assert_eq!(sem.available_permits(), 5);

Notify and Event​

AutoResetEvent​

Tokio's notify_one() wakes one waiter or stores one signal for a later wait. Asyncband's AutoResetEvent::set() does the same. When no waits are registered, repeated calls store just one signal:

- notify.notify_one();
- notify.notified().await;
+ event.set();
+ event.wait().await;

ManualResetEvent​

Tokio's notify_waiters() reaches Notified futures created before the call, even if they have never been polled. The call leaves no signal for a future created afterward:

use std::{future::Future, task::{Context, Poll, Waker}};

let mut cx = Context::from_waker(Waker::noop());
let notify = tokio::sync::Notify::new();
let mut before = Box::pin(notify.notified());
notify.notify_waiters();
let mut after = Box::pin(notify.notified());

assert_eq!(before.as_mut().poll(&mut cx), Poll::Ready(()));
assert_eq!(after.as_mut().poll(&mut cx), Poll::Pending);

Asyncband's ManualResetEvent stays set until reset(), so even a new wait can pass while the event is set. In the example below both waits are created before set(), but only one is polled and registered. That wait stays ready across the reset; the other first sees the event after it has been reset. A set()/reset() pair therefore cannot substitute for notify_waiters().

use std::{future::Future, task::{Context, Poll, Waker}};

let mut cx = Context::from_waker(Waker::noop());
let event = asyncband::event::ManualResetEvent::new();
let mut unpolled = Box::pin(event.wait());
let mut registered = Box::pin(event.wait());
assert_eq!(registered.as_mut().poll(&mut cx), Poll::Pending);

event.set();
event.wait().await; // A new wait passes while the event is set.
event.reset();

assert_eq!(registered.as_mut().poll(&mut cx), Poll::Ready(()));
assert_eq!(unpolled.as_mut().poll(&mut cx), Poll::Pending);

Once​

OnceCell​

Tokio's OnceCell::set(value) is synchronous. If another task is initializing the cell, it immediately returns SetError::InitializingError(value). Asyncband's once::OnceCell (feature once-cell) waits for that attempt. It can install value if the cell is still empty; otherwise it returns Err(value) with the unused input. Code that propagated Tokio's error with ? may need to handle that value explicitly or convert it to an application error.

use asyncband::once::OnceCell;

let cell = OnceCell::new();
cell.set(42).await.unwrap();

let rejected = cell.set(7).await.unwrap_err();
assert_eq!(rejected, 7);
assert_eq!(cell.get(), Some(&42));

SetOnce and Completion​

Tokio's SetOnce lets one task wait for a value set by another. Asyncband separates those roles: a single-use Completer publishes the value, and cloneable Completion handles observe it.

let cell = tokio::sync::SetOnce::new();
cell.set(42).unwrap();
assert_eq!(*cell.wait().await, 42);
let (completer, completion) = asyncband::completion::new();
let observer = completion.clone();
completer.complete(42).unwrap();
assert_eq!(*observer.wait().await.unwrap(), 42);

If the Completer is dropped without publishing, observers receive Abandoned. A Tokio SetOnce waiter would keep waiting if nobody set the value. For initialization with no stored value, Asyncband's once::Once (feature once) lets one task run the initializer with call_once() and others wait().await without supplying one.

Additional Asyncband APIs​

Shutdown​

If you used a closed semaphore to signal shutdown, give each worker a ShutdownGuard and let it select between the request and the permit. Here the semaphore has no permits. Awaiting shutdown requests shutdown and waits for all guards to drop; the worker takes the shutdown branch and drops its guard when it returns.

let sem = asyncband::semaphore::Semaphore::new(0);
let (shutdown, guard) = asyncband::shutdown::new();

let worker = async move {
    tokio::select! {
        _ = guard.shutdown_requested() => false,
        _permit = sem.acquire(1) => true,
    }
};

let (acquired, ()) = tokio::join!(worker, shutdown);
assert!(!acquired);

This cancels the participating worker's acquisition. It does not close the semaphore for other callers.

LazyCell​

An async LazyCell stores its initializer without starting it. Pin the cell to drive an inline async initializer with force_pin. If that call is cancelled, a later caller can resume the same initializer.

use asyncband::once::LazyCell;

let lazy = LazyCell::new(async || 42);
assert_eq!(LazyCell::get(&lazy), None);

let lazy = std::pin::pin!(lazy);
assert_eq!(*LazyCell::force_pin(lazy.as_ref()).await, 42);

OnceMap and Singleflight​

Use OnceMap::compute to retain a value by key. If the value itself is a Result, compute caches an Err just like any other value. Use try_compute when a failed load should be retried:

use asyncband::once::OnceMap;

let ports = OnceMap::new();
let invalid = ports.try_compute("http", async || "n/a".parse::<u16>()).await;
assert!(invalid.is_err());

let retry = ports.try_compute("http", async || "8080".parse::<u16>()).await;
assert_eq!(retry, Ok(8080));
assert_eq!(ports.get("http"), Some(8080));

If callers should share only in-flight work, use singleflight::Group. A call for the same key after the work completes starts a new computation.

Other coordination patterns​

  • Wait for workers: use a Latch for a fixed countdown, or a WaitGroup when workers join by cloning a handle and finish by dropping it.
  • Coordinate phases: a Phaser lets participants register and withdraw. Dropping a participant removes it from later phases and lets the current phase finish without waiting for its arrival.
  • Wait for a condition: a Condvar releases the mutex while waiting and reacquires it before rechecking the predicate.
  • Reuse resources: object pools can cap the number of managed connections in a bounded pool or keep idle buffers for reuse in an unbounded one.

entry.title: Using Semaphores to Control In-Flight Work
entry.summary: Use Asyncband's Semaphore to share concurrency limits, keep permits with the resources they account for, and reserve capacity for work of different sizes.
entry.content:
An asynchronous program can start work faster than the resources behind it can handle. Downloads compete for connections and bandwidth. Background jobs compete for CPU time. Buffered data occupies memory until its consumer finishes with it. A semaphore gives these operations a shared budget: work acquires permits before consuming capacity and returns them when that capacity becomes available again.

The useful questions are what one permit represents, which operations share the budget, and how long each operation holds its permits. This post works through those choices with Asyncband's Semaphore, including how Apache OpenDAL and prek use it.

The Asyncband APIs below are from version 0.7.3, with the semaphore feature enabled. The HTTP example uses reqwest; the semaphore itself is runtime-independent.

Share a budget across operations​

Suppose a client should perform at most eight downloads at once. Create one Semaphore::new(8) and share it across the calls that consume that budget. Each download acquires one permit. When all eight are held, another acquisition waits asynchronously until capacity becomes available.

use asyncband::semaphore::Semaphore;

async fn download(
    client: &reqwest::Client,
    slots: &Semaphore,
    url: &str,
) -> Result<Vec<u8>, reqwest::Error> {
    let _permit = slots.acquire(1).await;
    let response = client.get(url).send().await?.error_for_status()?;
    Ok(response.bytes().await?.to_vec())
}

acquire returns a guard. Keeping that guard in _permit holds the slot through the download, including reading the response body. Returning from the function drops the guard and gives the slot back, including on an error. There is no separate success or error branch that needs to release it manually.

The semaphore must live outside the individual calls. Creating a new semaphore inside download would give every call its own eight-slot budget. An Arc<Semaphore> lets independently owned tasks share the same budget; each task can borrow it for acquire or use acquire_owned when the permit itself must own a reference to the semaphore.

This is useful when work comes from several places. Apache OpenDAL's ConcurrentLimitLayer lets multiple operators share an Asyncband semaphore. The hook runner prek similarly passes one semaphore through project runs to limit concurrent hook execution. The scope of the shared semaphore determines the scope of the limit.

Eight slots limit simultaneous downloads. The number completed per second still depends on their duration. A policy expressed in requests per second needs a time-based rate limiter.

Keep the permit with the resource​

In the example above, the download ends when the response body has been read. A streaming API has a different lifetime: it can return a response while the caller is still receiving its body. Releasing a permit when the response is returned would leave that later transfer outside the budget.

OpenDAL handles this at its HTTP transport boundary. When an HTTP concurrency limit is configured, it acquires a permit before sending the request and moves the permit into a wrapper around the response body stream. The stream holds the permit until it is dropped. If sending the request fails, the local permit is dropped instead.

That ownership pattern also applies to a returned buffer or a queued job: put the permit in the object that owns the charged resource. If ownership moves to another task, move the permit with it. The function that acquired the permit may return long before the resource is released.

The download example's returned Vec<u8> illustrates the boundary. Its slot covers the transfer, but the caller can retain the downloaded bytes afterward. Limiting transfers alone does not bound retained memory.

Charge for the size of the work​

A permit can represent a byte of capacity instead of one operation. This matters when a small buffer and a large buffer should consume different amounts of a shared budget.

Here is a standalone example of a fixed payload budget. It reserves capacity before allocating a buffer and keeps the reservation with the returned value:

use std::sync::Arc;

use asyncband::semaphore::{OwnedSemaphorePermit, Semaphore};

struct BufferBudget {
    capacity: usize,
    available: Arc<Semaphore>,
}

struct BudgetedBuffer {
    data: Vec<u8>,
    _permit: OwnedSemaphorePermit,
}

impl BufferBudget {
    fn new(capacity: usize) -> Self {
        Self {
            capacity,
            available: Arc::new(Semaphore::new(capacity)),
        }
    }

    async fn allocate(&self, len: usize) -> Option<BudgetedBuffer> {
        if len > self.capacity {
            return None;
        }

        let permit = self.available.clone().acquire_owned(len).await;
        Some(BudgetedBuffer {
            data: vec![0; len],
            _permit: permit,
        })
    }
}

With BufferBudget::new(8 * 1024 * 1024), the budget covers eight MiB of payload. A 64 KiB allocation charges 64 KiB; a two MiB allocation charges two MiB. The buffer and its reservation can move together between tasks. Dropping the buffer frees its data and returns the permits.

Rejecting a request larger than the entire fixed budget is necessary: returning every outstanding permit could still never satisfy it. Reserve the full amount in one acquisition, too. Acquiring a large reservation incrementally can leave several callers each holding some capacity while all wait for the rest.

This budget counts the payload bytes in these buffers. Allocator overhead, other allocations, and extra copies require their own accounting. Growing or copying a buffer must reserve the additional capacity before doing so.

Decide what happens when capacity runs out​

Waiting is one admission policy. acquire(n).await waits for capacity; try_acquire(n) returns None when it cannot acquire the requested permits immediately. A caller can use the latter to reject or defer work instead of joining the wait queue. A deadline around acquire gives waiting a time limit.

The placement of the acquisition matters. If a program allocates a large payload and only then waits for its permit, that payload already consumes memory outside the budget. Likewise, spawning one task per incoming job and acquiring inside each task limits admitted work while allowing an arbitrarily large population of waiting tasks. Apply admission before creating the resource whose growth you intend to bound, or bound the waiting population separately.

Asyncband assigns permits to queued acquisitions in order. A large acquisition at the front can therefore hold back smaller ones behind it. If a budget has three units left and the first waiter needs five, a later one-unit waiter waits too. This preserves ordering, with a latency cost when request sizes vary substantially.

Dropping a pending acquisition removes it from the queue without leaking permits; retrying joins at the back. After acquisition completes, dropping the permit guard returns its permits. This accounting does not undo application side effects or stop work that has been handed to another task; the task doing that work must retain the permit for its actual lifetime.

Adjust a running budget​

Some applications change their concurrency budget while work is already running. Asyncband provides two operations for this: release(n) adds capacity, and reduce_permits(n) removes exactly n permits from the logical balance. A reduction does not revoke permits that callers already hold. If insufficient permits are currently available, later returns repay the deficit before ordinary queued acquisitions proceed.

For example, suppose an eight-slot budget is fully occupied and its controller reduces it by three. The eight operations can finish normally. As their guards are dropped, three returned permits retire the deficit; after all eight return, five slots remain available. The controller should serialize budget changes so that each adjustment is applied once.

drain_permits(n) only removes permits that are available at the time and returns the number removed. Draining three from that fully occupied budget removes zero, so it cannot promise the same capacity reduction. Also, returning an ordinary guard already restores its permits: an additional release would add capacity a second time.

For a fixed limit, acquiring and dropping guards is enough. Add weighted reservations or capacity adjustments when the resource being controlled calls for them, and keep the permit's lifetime aligned with the work it accounts for.
